name: Mt. Washington Auto Road Bicycle Hillclimb
start_location: Base of the Mt. Washington Auto Road, 1 Mt. Washington Auto Road (Route 16), Gorham, NH 03581
date_note: 2027 date not yet announced. The 2026 race (the 53rd) was Saturday, August 15 with a Sunday rain date. Registration for the following year opens January 1 for returning and special-category riders and January 15 for the general public.
typical_timing: A Saturday in mid-August, with a Sunday rain date
registration_note: Registration is on BikeReg. It opens January 1 for returning and special-category riders and January 15 for everyone else, and closes in early August. Two entry options: a flat fee, or a lower fee plus a fundraising minimum for Tin Mountain, with the shortfall charged to your card on August 1. You must have a driver to bring you and your bike down; riding down is prohibited.

distances.label: 7.6 miles
distances.note: One way, all uphill, base to the 6,288 ft summit. Average grade 12%, extended sections at 18%, last 50 yards at 22%.

terrain: Paved mountain toll road, 7.6 miles at an average 12% grade with no flat sections; finishes above treeline.
cost: $350 flat entry, or $150 plus a fundraising minimum for Tin Mountain (2025 pricing)
summary: The Mt. Washington Auto Road Bicycle Hillclimb is a 7.6-mile race up the Mt. Washington Auto Road in Gorham, New Hampshire, to the 6,288-foot summit, the highest point in the northeastern United States. The road averages 12% with pitches to 22%. It has run since 1973, is held on a Saturday in mid-August, takes up to about 600 riders, and is the main fundraiser for Tin Mountain Conservation Center, which has organized it since 1990. It is the one day a year the road is closed to cars for bikes.
history: The Auto Road opened in August 1861 as a carriage road to the summit. The bicycle hillclimb started in 1973, 112 years later. The 2026 race was the 53rd.

In 1990 the Auto Road asked Tin Mountain Conservation Center, a nonprofit environmental education group in the area, to organize the race. It has run it since, and net proceeds fund Tin Mountain's programs for children, adults and families.

Weather has cancelled the race outright in 1994, 1995, 2007 and 2023, and COVID cancelled 2020. Course records were reset in 2022 after the road was fully paved; as of 2025 they stood at 50:15 for men (Ian Boswell) and 58:01 for women (Illi Gardner). Earlier records set by Tyler Hamilton and Geneviève Jeanson were struck in 2011 after both admitted doping. The event keeps a 'Rockpiler' list of riders with ten or more finishes.
what_to_expect: Race-day registration runs 6:15 to 7:45 AM at the base and the road closes to cars at 8:00 AM. Six waves go off five minutes apart starting at 8:30, top racers first, then age groups. Timing ends 3 hours 5 minutes after the start, at 12:05 PM.

The road never eases. It averages 12%, has long stretches at 18%, and the final 50 yards to the line are 22%. Above treeline it is exposed, and even in August it can be wet, windy and cold; the summit is known for the worst weather in America. Front and tail lights are recommended because of fog. Riders often bring very low gears.

You must have a driver. Bikes are not allowed to descend the road, so your driver takes an Auto Pass from your bib, drives up after the race, and brings you down when the road reopens around noon. Drivers should expect four to five hours at the summit. Finishers get a fleece blanket and medal, and there is an awards ceremony about 1:15 PM. The base area has a pre-race mechanic (REI Co-op) and lunch tickets; no dogs.
weather_note: At the summit, August averages a high of about 54°F and a low of about 43°F, with a record August low of 20°F. Down at the base in Gorham it is a normal New England August day. The organizer's own line is that 'even August days can be wet, windy and cold' up top, so pack a hat, gloves and a warm jacket for after the finish. Weather has cancelled the race in 1994, 1995, 2007 and 2023.
